builds.title: Levels, the gunsmith and split squads
builds.summary: Your own character now levels up and spends talent points, and earns shillings in the night to spend at the village gunsmith on new guns and upgrades. In multiplayer each player commands their own squad, village women heal the wounded, killing head shots burst heads, and each line's gates move every night.
changes: Earn experience and level up your own character, then spend talent points in three trees (Marksman, Brawler, Officer) with K.
Earn shillings in the night and run back to the village gunsmith for a revolver, shotgun, lever-action rifle or scoped sniper rifle, plus weapon upgrades and supplies.
In multiplayer the company is split into squads, one per player, each holding its own stretch of line under its own orders. The Tab roster now ranks the players by kills.
Five village women (Camille, Regan, Kara, Jessie and Yuriko) tend the wounds of anyone who comes near them, and the Village Palisade is twice as strong.
A killing head shot bursts the head in a spray of blood.
Each line's gates fall in different places every night, so the dead take a different road.

design.q: How do squads hold the line in multiplayer?
design.a: Each squad holds its own line and moves independently.

design.q: How should talents be organised?
design.a: Three trees (Marksman, Brawler, Officer) with five tiers each, opened with K.

design.q: What carries over between nights?
design.a: Level, talents, money and guns all carry over for the campaign. In multiplayer they're kept per player name; a retry restores them and a new campaign resets them.

design.q: Where do bought guns go?
design.a: A new slot 6, one gun at a time; buying another swaps it.

design.q: Where do players shop?
design.a: A gunsmith stall in the village: press E there during the night, or use it at dawn.

design.q: How do players earn money?
design.a: Kills plus small bonuses: walker 2, runner 3, brute 10, plus revives and repairs.

design.q: How are the men split between players?
design.a: Single player is unchanged. Multiplayer deals the men out evenly by role, reshuffles when a player joins or leaves, and a man a player takes over leaves the squad.

design.q: What does the leaderboard show?
design.a: Kills and level: name, level, kills tonight and kills this campaign, sorted by kills.

builds.title: Pipes and bayonets
builds.summary: The bagpipe now steadies the men within its reach and drives their fixed bayonets 35% harder. Holding an instrument shows all its boosts on screen.
changes: The bagpipe now steadies the men: everyone within its 14 m reach regains morale while you play.
Men within the pipe's reach hit 35% harder with fixed bayonets.
Holding an instrument now shows all its boosts (reloading, morale and bayonets) at the bottom right.

design.q: What should the bagpipe do?
design.a: It should regenerate company morale within its aura radius and boost bayonet damage by +35%.

design.q: How fast should the pipe restore morale?
design.a: 1.0 per second, a little below the drum's 1.5 because the pipe reaches much further. The best tune nearby counts; they don't stack.

design.q: When does the bayonet bonus apply?
design.a: Only with bayonets fixed, for the militia's stabs and a player's bayonet thrust. Butt strikes and the saber aren't boosted.

design.q: Should the new boosts show in the UI?
design.a: Yes, the same way the reload bonus shows: all of an instrument's boosts are listed under its name while you hold or play it.

builds.title: Character screen and company card
builds.summary: Before joining a multiplayer lobby you now name your man and choose how he looks, and everyone in the company sees him that way. While the company musters, a card shows how many players have joined, and who.
changes: Choosing Multiplayer opens a character screen: name your man (a name is now required) and pick his skin tone, height, build and hair.
A turning 3D preview shows your man as you change him, and your choices are remembered.
Everyone in the company sees each player's man the way they made him.
While the company musters, a card shows how many players have joined, and who.
The info panel shows the player count during the night.

design.q: When does the character screen appear?
design.a: Every time you choose Multiplayer, before the lobby list, filled in with your saved choices.

design.q: What can you change?
design.a: Skin tone, height, build (fatness) and hair style. Name is a forced input: you can't reach the lobbies without one.

design.q: Where does the host see how many people are in the lobby?
design.a: On the pre-night screen, where a lobby opens once its server is up: a card beside the orders with the count, the names and the open places. Every player sees it, and the count is also in the info panel during the night.

design.q: Coat and hair colour?
design.a: Not separate choices. A saved seed keeps them the same between the preview and the game, and Randomise re-rolls them.

builds.title: Hold-E freeze fix and multiplayer diagnostics
builds.summary: Fixes the freeze some players saw while holding E to repair or revive on slower computers, and adds an F3 network diagnostics overlay for multiplayer.
changes: Fixed the freeze while holding E to repair or revive on slower computers: the game no longer loses updates and jumps forward when you let go.
Holding a key no longer floods the browser with repeat key presses during play.
Press F3 in multiplayer to show network diagnostics: updates received and applied per second, frame rate and stalls.
Multiplayer is kept for the newest version and the one before it; older builds on this site are single player only.
Add ?diag=1 to the game's address to open the diagnostics as soon as the game starts.

design.q: Should we dig into the code to find the cause of the freeze?
design.a: Yes, investigate.

design.q: What happens during the freeze?
design.a: The camera still turns. It unfreezes and everything jumps forward when E is released. It happened in Chrome on a slower Windows machine; a faster Mac didn't freeze.

design.q: Should test players be sent into a real lobby to reproduce it?
design.a: Yes: three browser players started a lobby and played it to look for latency problems.

design.q: Rerun with a pasted console logger, or add diagnostics to the game?
design.a: Add in-game diagnostics.

design.q: Is this a new version or a maintenance change?
design.a: A new version, since it changes the game build.

design.q: Add the buffer fix and the key-repeat filter to v5?
design.a: Yes, add both to v5.

design.q: How many versions keep multiplayer?
design.a: The newest and the one before it; older builds keep single player.

design.q: Add a slow-machine safeguard, or ship as is?
design.a: Ship as is: the Windows machine ran at 60 FPS with no stalls in Edge, so Chrome's graphics setup there was the cause.

builds.title: Knockback, power-ups, emotes, instruments and watchtowers
builds.summary: Hits from the dead now shove you back, brutes drop power-ups, and a weapon bar adds a saber and instruments that speed up reloading around you. Watchtowers stand between the lines to climb and fire from, and you can emote while you wait for the next wave.
changes: Zombie hits now shove you back (harder from a brute), and the health bar shows each hit draining away.
Brutes sometimes drop a carpenter's kit, fresh powder or a rum flask. Walk over it to help the whole line.
A weapon bar (1–6): a saber, and a drum, bagpipe and flute that make the men around you reload faster while you play.
A watchtower stands between each pair of lines: climb it to fire over the walls, but the dead will try to bring it down.
Hold Z for emotes: smoke a cigarette, dance a jig, cheer, salute and more.
A ring around the crosshair shows your reload closing in.

design.q: Should all six features work in multiplayer too, or single player first?
design.a: Full multiplayer: they run on the server and show for every player.

design.q: What goes in weapon bar slot 6?
design.a: Leave it empty and greyed out for now.

design.q: Which brute power-ups should ship?
design.a: The carpenter's kit, fresh powder and the rum flask.

builds.title: Web browser multiplayer
builds.summary: Up to five players can now hold the line together from their browsers, with a lobby browser for starting or joining a company, and anyone who falls can be revived by a comrade.
changes: Multiplayer: up to 5 players hold the line together, in the browser or on the desktop.
A lobby browser on the new main menu: join an open lobby or start your own, even in the middle of a night.
The host is the sergeant, giving the orders and spending the supplies at dawn. Each extra player brings more of the dead.
Revive the fallen: hold E on a fallen man within a minute to get him back on his feet, in single player too.
A downed player can wait for a comrade to revive them, or press Space to take over the nearest man.
Smooth over laggy connections: the dead and your comrades move steadily, sprinting no longer snaps you back, and zombies strike where you really are.

design.q: Who can call the line's orders?
design.a: Lobby host only.

design.q: How do players fit into the 20-man company?
design.a: Added on top, with harder waves.

design.q: Who spends supplies at dawn?
design.a: The host decides.

design.q: Can players join once a night has started?
design.a: Drop in anytime.

design.q: What happens when a player falls?
design.a: Add a revive feature: for up to a minute after a militiaman falls, a player can revive him by holding E on him for 10 seconds. If he isn't revived, the player jumps into the nearest living AI man, so deaths still drain the company.

design.q: Who can be revived?
design.a: Players and AI men.

design.q: What does a downed player do while waiting?
design.a: Wait, or give up early. It happens automatically at 60 s.

design.q: What happens when the host disconnects?
design.a: Host passes on to the longest-connected player.

design.q: Single player?
design.a: Keep offline single player.

design.q: Players who join stutter and zombies lurch: what should change?
design.a: Draw the world a moment in the past between snapshots, give the server's speed check a catch-up allowance with eased corrections, and have zombies strike where a remote player really is.

builds.title: Five nights at the Hollow
builds.summary: Fort Hollow becomes a five-night campaign: gates in every line, bayonet charges, and a company of musketmen, riflemen, grenadiers and a drummer who level up between nights, and can break and run.
changes: A five-night campaign. At each dawn, spend supplies on stronger works, iron-bound gates, paper cartridges, rum, recruits, riflemen, grenadiers or a second drummer
Two gates in every line: the men march through them, you can't cross the walls, and the dead go first for any gate near them, since it's weaker than the wall
New orders: G advances the whole line and B fixes bayonets (deadly up close, slower reloads); fix them and advance to charge. F is your own bayonet thrust

Four roles, levels that carry between nights, and morale that breaks. The drummer walks the line to steady every man on it, and routed men run for the village and rally once calm. Hold Tab to see the company
Brutes reel back when hit, and a realism pass gives jointed figures in period dress, textured timber, grass, stars, ground mist and filmic lighting. The HUD now scales with the window

design.q: Should falling back be all-or-nothing, or partial?
design.a: Full fall backs, plus a fix-bayonets command and a move-forward command. These became two separate orders (B and G) that combine into a bayonet charge.

design.q: Are you a sergeant giving orders, or an ordinary soldier?
design.a: An ordinary soldier.

design.q: As an ordinary soldier, who gives the line's orders?
design.a: You still call them, with no rank: same stats as any man, and you take over another man's musket when you fall.

design.q: How should barricades and gates work?
design.a: Two gates for defenders on each line. The dead prioritise crushing a gate when it's near them, and gates have less health than wall sections.

design.q: One night, or a longer campaign?
design.a: Several nights, with upgrades in between: five nights and eight upgrades.

design.q: Should militiamen level up, have roles, or have morale that can break?
design.a: All three.

design.q: Keep the low-poly look, or go more realistic?
design.a: A more realistic feel.

design.q: Realism through CC0 animated models, or better procedural art?
design.a: CC0 animated models were chosen, but the model download was then declined, so this version does a deeper procedural pass instead.

design.q: How should the drummer's boost reach the men?
design.a: He walks the back of the line from end to end, so the whole line gets his boost.

design.q: Should hits affect brutes physically?
design.a: Yes: big zombies are knocked back when hit.

design.q: What should the zombies sound like?
design.a: More guttural and less computer-like, with each zombie's pitch varied. The synthesised voices sounded like jets, so zombie sounds are removed for now; a README concept covers bringing them back.

builds.title: First muster
builds.summary: The first playable night: twenty militiamen hold four lines against the dead from sunset to dawn, firing in volleys and falling back west toward the village.
changes: Four destructible north–south lines: split-rail fence, log breastwork, stake stockade and the village palisade
Twenty AI militiamen who make ready, present and fire in volleys, then reload
First-person musket with aim-down-sights and headshots; fire with the line for +50% damage
Hold E to repair or rebuild broken barricade sections; T orders the line to fall back
Seven waves of walkers, runners and brutes across a sunset-to-dawn night
If you fall, you take up the musket of the nearest man still standing
